title: Carlston Annis Shell Mound
summary: In Butler County, Carlston Annis is a Late Archaic shell midden built up by mussel gatherers between roughly 3000 and 1000 BC, with 390 human burials.
bodyMarkdown:
The Carlston Annis Shell Mound (15Bt5) is a large Archaic period shell midden in Butler County. Over many centuries, Native people who gathered freshwater mussels piled their shells here, lived on the growing mound and buried their dead in it. It is one of the best-studied Archaic shell middens in Kentucky.

## The mound

An account of [the Carlston Annis Shell Mound](https://grokipedia.com/page/carlston_annis_shell_mound) gives its size as about 350 by 300 feet. It rises about 6 feet above the surrounding ground, but the shell runs 7.5 feet deep at the center. The difference comes from floods that have laid soil around the base since the midden formed. Because it is the highest point nearby, its top usually stays dry when the land around it floods.

## Excavation

Sources give different dates for the main excavation. University of Kentucky archaeologists began digging in 1939 under W. D. Funkhouser and W. S. Webb. The same article, citing another study, says Works Progress Administration workers excavated it between 1937 and 1941. Both dates are shown here because the sources do not agree. The mound had also been test excavated in the 1920s.

Before the dig, neighbors often took shell from the mound's edges to use as chicken feed. The excavators laid a trench through the southern part and then dug the mound in blocks.

## The people of the midden

The excavation found 390 human burials and 28 dog burials. Ages ranged from infants to adults. More than half the burials, 215, had objects with them, most of them personal items such as shell gorgets, beads and hairpins.

Overall life expectancy at birth was a little over twenty years. Children under five made up 29.7 percent of the skeletons, nearly three-quarters of them infants.

The site produced 19,733 artifacts. Bone tools included more than 1,000 awls and 900 fishhooks. Carlston Annis was the first Kentucky shell midden where fishhooks made by one particular method were found. Plant remains show a diet rich in nuts, with hickory nuts making up about 80 percent of the identifiable remains.

## Dates

Radiocarbon dating suggests some artifacts are as old as 5424 BC, though most date between 3200 and 1400 BC. A few later points, one Adena and some Mississippian, and 65 pottery sherds show that later peoples also camped on the high ground. Two Paleoindian fluted points lay beneath the mound and predate it.

## Kentucky today

Carlston Annis was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in April 1986, one of 24 Archaic shell middens listed together. In 1994 several of the middens became a National Historic Landmark district. Related stories include Indian Knoll and [Chiggerville](/stories/chiggerville-15oh1/). The mound is an archaeological site and its burials deserve respect.
